en.t: will he be pleased with you

01.n: The particle can mean 'when' or 'if', and the translations divide.

02.r: Bringing an animal to the altar.
02.n: Literally 'make come near', the causative of a verb Gesenius gives as TO DRAW NEAR, TO APPROACH. It is a different verb from 'bring near' later in the verse, so we render it 'present' to keep the two apart. This first form has an extra final letter, which the brief marks as emphatic.

03.n: The adjective stands alone, 'a blind (one)'; the context shows it is an animal. There is no article.

04.n: An infinitive with 'to'. Gesenius: to slaughter animals, and specially to slay in sacrifice.

05.r: Puts the offerers' conduct to the test.
05.n: Literally 'there is no evil'; the Hebrew has no question marker, and Hebrew can leave a question unmarked. The KJV, DRC and BSB read a question; the ASV and JPS an exclamation, 'it is no evil!'; YLT the offerers' own words, 'There is no evil'.

06.n: Gesenius: evil, bad, and lists the word used physically of animals, 'bad cattle', as well as morally. Both senses meet here: a bad animal, and an evil act.

08.r: Bringing an animal to the altar.
08.n: The same verb as 'present' at the start of the verse.

09.r: An animal that cannot walk soundly.
09.n: Gesenius: lame. Again the adjective stands alone, with no article.

10.n: A participle of a verb meaning to be weak, to be sick. Gesenius gives the senses to be worn down in strength, to be infirm, to be sick.

13.r: A challenge: try giving it to the governor.
13.n: The causative of the verb 'come near', the usual word for presenting an offering; we render it 'bring near' to keep it apart from 'present' earlier in the verse. The challenge is ironic: no one would dare give such a gift to a governor.

14.r: Softens the command, here with irony.
14.n: Gesenius: a particle used in submissive and modest request, in English 'now', as a word of entreaty. The KJV says 'now', YLT 'I pray thee'.

15.r: The provincial governor, whose favour mattered.
15.n: Gesenius: the governor of a province, ranking below a satrap. The 'your' is singular: each offerer is addressed in turn.

s: will he be pleased with you
16.r: Would the governor receive you kindly with such a gift?
16.n: Gesenius gives the root sense TO BE DELIGHTED with someone, and a special sense, to receive graciously someone who brings gifts.
t: will he be pleased with thee
will he be content with thee
if he will be pleased with it
will he be pleased with thee
will he be pleased with thee
Would he be pleased with you

18.r: Would he receive you with favour?
18.n: To 'lift up the face' of someone is to receive him with favour, as the BSB gives it, 'show you favor'. The KJV and others say 'accept thy person'.

19.r: The offerer himself, as he stands before the governor.
19.n: The noun is plural in form; Gesenius notes that it is not used in the singular.

20.r: Marks the words as the LORD's.
20.n: The verb is a perfect, 'has said', the standing formula for the LORD's words; YLT renders 'Said'.

21.r: The personal name of Israel's God.

22.r: The LORD as commander of armies.
22.n: Gesenius: an army, a host; BDB notes its use in the name of the LORD as God of war. The Greek translators wrote 'Almighty'.

_extra.16: A stray question mark that our digital Greek text counts as a word; there is nothing to pair.

01.n: διότι ἐὰν, 'for if': the Greek has 'for' in place of 'and'.

02.n: προσάγω, to bring to, to present. The Greek uses this one verb for both Hebrew verbs in the verse, 'present' and 'bring near', so it does not keep them apart.

04.n: εἰς θυσίαν, 'for a sacrifice', a noun where the Hebrew has a verb.

10.n: ἢ ἄρρωστον, 'or sick': the Greek has 'or' for 'and'.

14.n: δή, 'then, now', a particle of urging.

15.n: Dictionary form supplied; the brief gives none. ἡγουμένῳ is the participle of ἡγέομαι, to lead, used as a noun: 'your leader'.

17.n: The Greek repeats 'if' for 'or': 'if he will receive you, if he will accept your face'.

19.n: λήμψεται πρόσωπον, 'receive the face': the Greek keeps the Hebrew idiom. The New Testament word for partiality, προσωπολημψία, is built from this phrase.

22.n: Παντοκράτωρ, 'Almighty', for 'of hosts': the same word the New Testament uses for God as the Almighty.
